bigPicture.subtitle: The Cross in the Most Ambitious City in Greece
paragraphs: Stand on the narrow neck of land that joins mainland Greece to the Peloponnese and you are standing in the most strategic four miles of the ancient Mediterranean. On the west, the port of Lechaeum faces Italy. On the east, the port of Cenchreae faces Asia. Between them ran the diolkos, a paved stone trackway on which ships were dragged overland on wheeled platforms so captains could avoid the deadly voyage around the southern cape. Every cargo, every sailor, every new idea and every new god crossed that isthmus — and the city that sat on it took a cut of all of it. That city was Corinth. And around AD 50 a tentmaker with a recent beating behind him walked into it alone.

This was not old Greek Corinth. The Roman general Lucius Mummius had levelled that city in 146 BC, and for a century the site lay largely empty. Then in 44 BC Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony and filled it with freed slaves, veterans, and ambitious nobodies. Within a hundred years it was the capital of the province of Achaia, rich, loud, and new money to its bones — a city where nobody's grandfather had been anybody, and where everybody was therefore desperate to be seen as someone. Status was the air Corinth breathed. Men erected inscriptions to their own generosity. Orators were followed like celebrities. The Isthmian Games, second only to Olympia, were held a few miles away every two years. (You will hear one honest caution in this study more than once: the famous claim that a thousand temple prostitutes worked the shrine of Aphrodite on the Acrocorinth comes from the geographer Strabo and describes the older Greek city, and many historians doubt it for the Roman one. You do not need the legend. The letter itself tells you plainly enough what Corinth was like.)

Paul stayed eighteen months — “He lived there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them” (Acts 18:11) — longer than almost anywhere else he planted. He worked with his hands beside Aquila and Priscilla, refugees from Claudius' expulsion of the Jews from Rome. The ruler of the synagogue, Crispus, believed with his whole household. And when the proconsul Gallio threw the case against Paul out of court, he left historians a gift: an inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio's term in Achaia to around AD 51–52, which makes Paul's time in Corinth one of the firmest fixed points in the entire chronology of the New Testament. Then Paul left. And a few years later, from Ephesus across the Aegean (16:8), he received news that broke his heart.

The news came from three directions. People from Chloe's household reported quarrels (1:11). There were rumours of something worse — a sexual sin the pagans themselves would not tolerate (5:1). And a delegation arrived with a letter from the church full of questions — about marriage, about meat offered to idols, about spiritual gifts, about the collection — which Paul answers one by one, marking each with the same little phrase, “Now concerning…” (7:1, 7:25, 8:1, 12:1, 16:1, 16:12). He had already written them once; that earlier letter is lost (5:9). So 1 Corinthians is not a treatise. It is a pastor's reply to an inbox — and that is exactly why it is the most practical book Paul ever wrote. Here is the church at its most gifted and its most carnal at the same time: speaking in tongues and suing each other, celebrating the Lord's Supper while the poor went home hungry, proud of their tolerance while one of their members slept with his father's wife.

And into that city of climbers Paul carried one message, and refused to dress it up: “For I determined not to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (2:2). Every problem in the letter is answered from that one place. Factions? Was Paul crucified for you? Lawsuits? You were bought with a price. Pride in knowledge? The brother for whose sake Christ died. Chaos in worship? The love that does not seek its own way. Denial of the resurrection? Then Christ is not raised, and you are still in your sins. Sixteen chapters, a dozen pastoral crises, and one cross standing in the middle of all of them. If Romans showed you the gospel as a cathedral, 1 Corinthians shows you the gospel as a hospital — and the patients are people exactly like you.

bridge.intro: The Holy Spirit placed 1 Corinthians directly after Romans, and the order is deliberate even though it is not the order of the calendar. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians first — from Ephesus, around AD 54 — and wrote Romans two or three years later, sitting inside the very church this letter is trying to rescue. The canon reverses them so that you learn the doctrine before you watch it tested:

points.title: From Strangers to Children
points.body: Romans is a letter of introduction to a church Paul had never visited, and it reads like it: carefully argued, courteous, laying out the gospel in order so that strangers could trust him. First Corinthians is written to people he personally brought to Christ, and it reads like a father at the kitchen table. “I don’t write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News” (4:14–15). In Romans Paul persuades. In Corinth he pleads, warns, rebukes, teases, threatens a rod and offers gentleness in the same sentence (4:21). The shift teaches you something before you read a single chapter: truth that was proclaimed to strangers has to be lived out among family, and family is where it gets hard.

points.title: From the Doctrine to the Floor
points.body: Romans 6 told you that your old self was crucified with Christ and that you must not let sin reign in your mortal body. First Corinthians shows you what that sounds like in a congregation where a man has taken his father's wife, believers are dragging each other before pagan judges, and some members are visiting prostitutes and calling it freedom. Paul's answer is Romans 6 spoken in the past tense to real people with real histories: “Such were some of you, but you were washed. But you were sanctified. But you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God” (6:11). Notice the order. Justification is the last verb in the sentence, not the first — because these people already knew the doctrine. What they had lost was the connection between the doctrine and their bodies.

points.title: One Body — First Drawn, Then Bleeding
points.body: In Romans the body of Christ is a calm sentence: “For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function, so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another” (Romans 12:4–5). In 1 Corinthians that same body is torn and arguing. The word Paul uses in his opening appeal is σχίσμα (schísma, G4978) — a rip in a garment — “that there be no divisions among you” (1:10). Chapter 12 then takes the Romans sentence and turns it into a full-length anatomy lesson, with an eye telling a hand it is not needed and a foot sulking because it is not a hand. Romans gave you the doctrine of the body. Corinth shows you what happens when gifted members forget it, and chapter 13 is the cure written between the two chapters on gifts.

points.title: The Weak Brother, Now With a Menu
points.body: Romans 14 laid down the principle about food and conscience: “Don’t destroy with your food him for whom Christ died” (Romans 14:15). Corinth is where that principle has to survive an actual dinner invitation — meat that had been offered in a pagan temple and then sold in the market, or served at a feast in the temple's own dining rooms. Paul answers with the same phrase, almost word for word: “And through your knowledge, he who is weak perishes, the brother for whose sake Christ died” (8:11). The knowledge the strong were proud of was correct. Their love was missing. Romans gave you the rule. First Corinthians shows you the cost of keeping it — and Paul's own decision, which ought to stop you cold: “Therefore if food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat forever more” (8:13).

coreTheme.title: We Preach Christ Crucified — the Power of God and the Wisdom of God
paragraphs: The whole letter turns on one blunt sentence: “For Jews ask for signs, Greeks seek after wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified; a stumbling block to Jews, and foolishness to Greeks, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1:22–24). Feel how offensive that was. The cross, σταυρός (staurós, G4716), was not jewellery in the first century. It was the most degrading death Rome had — reserved for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals, so shameful that polite Romans avoided even speaking of it. Paul walks into the most status-hungry city in Greece and announces that God's wisdom is a crucified Jew. To a Greek that is μωρία (mōría, G3472) — the root of our word moron. It is the dumbest thing a man could say in public.

And Paul does not soften it. He leans into it. “I determined not to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (2:2) is not a description of a narrow preaching style; it is a strategy. He came, he says, “in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling” (2:3) — deliberately without the polished rhetoric Corinth paid to hear — “that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God” (2:5). If the gospel had been sold to them with brilliance, it could be bought back from them by someone more brilliant. A faith that rests on a performance is always one better performance away from collapse.

Watch the cross answer every problem in the book. The Corinthians were boasting about their leaders; the cross says God chose the foolish, the weak, the despised and the things that are not, “that no flesh should boast before God” (1:29). They were proud of their freedom; the cross says “you were bought with a price” (6:20). They were proud of their knowledge; the cross says the weak brother is one “for whose sake Christ died” (8:11). They were turning the Lord's Supper into a status meal; the cross says “you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (11:26). Some were denying the resurrection; the cross and the empty tomb are “first of all” (15:3), the thing on which everything else stands or falls.

Paul never got over it. Years later he wrote to the Galatians, “But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). And he wrote to Rome from the same city of Corinth, “I am not ashamed of the Good News of Christ, because it is the power of God for salvation” (Romans 1:16) — the very word, δύναμις (dýnamis, G1411), that he uses here in 1:18 and 1:24. Corinth taught him that the cross is not merely how you get into the Christian life. It is the measuring rod for every decision inside it. Read every chapter of this letter with one question: where is the cross in this? Because Paul always knows, and by chapter 16 you will too.

truths.intro: As we journey through these 16 chapters, the Holy Spirit wants to anchor these truths in your spirit:

items.title: You Belong to Christ — Not to a Personality
items.body: The first sin Paul addresses is not immorality. It is fan clubs. “Each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ’” (1:12). Corinth had turned its teachers into celebrities and its church into competing brands, and Paul attacks it before anything else because it is the root of everything else. His answer is staggering: “Therefore let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. All are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (3:21–23). You do not belong to the preacher. The preacher belongs to you — a gift God gave for your growth. And you belong to Christ. Any loyalty that competes with that, however spiritual it sounds, is the first crack in a split church.

items.title: Your Body Is Not Your Own
items.body: Corinth had a slogan, and Paul quotes it back to them twice: “All things are lawful for me” (6:12; 10:23). Many in the church apparently believed that what you did with your body did not touch your spirit — the body was a shell, temporary and unimportant. Paul flattens that idea with a doctrine the Greek world found absurd: the body is going to be raised. “Now God raised up the Lord, and will also raise us up by his power” (6:14). So the body matters forever. “Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body” (6:19–20). This is the sentence that makes holiness physical. It reaches your sexuality, your appetite, your rest, your phone, and your habits, and it tells you that every one of them belongs to Someone who paid for them with blood.

items.title: Nothing Done in Love Is Ever Wasted
items.body: The Corinthians had every gift and very little love. They spoke in tongues, prophesied, knew mysteries — and Paul tells them that without ἀγάπη (agápē, G26), all of it is “sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal” (13:1). The great love chapter was not written for a wedding. It was written as a rebuke to gifted people who were using their gifts to rank each other. And then, two chapters later, Paul gives love its eternal reason. Because Christ is raised, the dead will be raised, the perishable will put on the imperishable, and death itself will be swallowed up. “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (15:58). Put chapters 13 and 15 together and you have the whole ethic of the Christian life: love is the only thing that lasts, and the resurrection guarantees that not one act of it will be lost.

preparation.intro: Before we step into Chapter 1, prepare your spirit with these reflections:

items.title: The Name on Your Banner
items.body: Every Corinthian faction would have told you their loyalty was spiritual. The Paul group loved the founder. The Apollos group loved good teaching. The Cephas group loved the original apostles. And the Christ group — the most dangerous of all — loved being above the other three. Before you begin, ask honestly: whose name do you quietly carry? A ministry, a preacher, a denomination, a style of worship, a stream of teaching you consider superior? None of those is wrong to value. But if you would feel more loyalty to it than to a brother who belongs to a different one, you are standing in Corinth. Write down the name, and hold it loosely before chapter 1 asks you, “Is Christ divided?”

items.title: The Thing You Call Freedom
items.body: “All things are lawful for me” was not a pagan slogan. It was a Christian one — very likely a twisted echo of Paul's own preaching about grace. Which means the most dangerous lies in this letter are half-truths that started in the pulpit. So name the area of your life where you have been saying, in effect, “I am free; it doesn’t matter.” What you watch, what you drink, how you spend, where you go, who you are alone with. Paul will not answer you with a list of rules. He will answer you with two questions you should begin asking now: does it build up, and will it bring me under its power? Hold that area before God as you read, and let the letter do its surgery.

prayerOfActivation: “Father, I come into this letter as a Corinthian. I live in a world that runs on status, that rewards the clever and the impressive, that tells me my worth depends on being seen — and I confess that much of that world lives in me. I have boasted in men. I have carried names and loyalties that divided me from my brothers and sisters. I have called things freedom that were really chains. I have known the right answers and loved too little. So before I read the first verse, I bring You the one thing this letter will keep pointing me to: the cross of Your Son. Let me determine, like Paul, not to know anything except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. Where my faith rests on the wisdom of men, move it onto the power of God. Where I have been proud of my gifts, show me that without love I am nothing but noise. Where I have treated my body as my own, remind me that I was bought with a price, and teach me to glorify You in it. Holy Spirit, You are the One who searches all things, even the deep things of God — open these sixteen chapters to me. Heal what is divided in me and in Your church. And by the time I reach the last chapter, let me be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in Your work, knowing that my labor is not in vain in You. In Jesus' name, Amen.”
